co_left_side_4.blurb: Left Side is the left-hand end of Dry Creek Crag, a short sandstone cliff in the desert country outside Montrose. About two dozen of its routes are bolted and a handful are trad, with a few that can be rigged for top-roping. Grades start near 5.3 and reach into the low 5.12s, but the heart of the wall is 5.8 to 5.10, so it suits a mixed group better than a hard-only crag. Some lines are noticeably steeper than the rest. Walls here are only around 30 to 50 feet tall, which keeps laps quick, and the cliff swings from shade to sun as the day wears on.
co_left_side_4.parking_note: A rough dirt road runs most of the way to the cliff rim; a high-clearance vehicle can park right at the top, while a low car has to stop short and walk a long way in.

co_little_scraggy_dome.blurb: Little Scraggy Dome is a quiet granite slab in the Buffalo Creek area of the South Platte, southwest of Denver. The climbing is mostly trad on friction slabs and cracks, with a couple of bolted lines and a good number of boulder problems at the base. Roped routes run from 5.8 through the 5.10s and into 5.11 and 5.12, while the problems span V1 up to the double digits, so there is a lot of range for such a small formation. Because the face points west, mornings stay cool in summer and afternoons are the warm choice in the colder months. Expect remote, uncrowded climbing with the usual Platte run-outs.

co_bang_s_canyon.blurb: Bang's Canyon is a recreation canyon on the south side of Grand Junction, and its climbing centers on a small, very steep wall near an abandoned mica mine. Most of the roped climbing is bolted and demanding: a lone 5.11 warm-up and a couple of 5.10s sit alongside a run of routes from 5.12 into the 5.13s, which makes it a strong training venue for strong climbers. Trad lines, a few aid routes and some V6 and V7 boulder problems round out the canyon. The cliff looks loose and dark from the trail but climbs technically, and the canyon catches afternoon shade. Plan on a real walk in from the road.
co_bang_s_canyon.parking_note: Leave the car at the gravel lot where the Rough and Bang's Canyon turnoff meets CS Road (Little Park Road), roughly five miles past the top of the hill; it doubles as a trailhead for a long-distance trail.
co_bang_s_canyon.approach: Follow a rough road southwest for about a quarter mile to a small side canyon, bear right (left goes into Rough Canyon) and keep walking up the drainage for 20 to 30 minutes to an old mica mine, a big pale cave. The sport wall sits a short way past it on the right.

co_cynical_pinnacle.blurb: Cynical Pinnacle is the most striking tower in the Cathedral Spires, a cluster of clean granite in the South Platte near Buffalo Creek and Pine. It is overwhelmingly a trad destination, with long crack and chimney lines from 5.8 through the low 5.13s; the bulk of the routes sit between 5.10 and 5.12, while a few are bolted, one is aid and one is a top-rope. Many climbs are multi-pitch, and the best-known lines have drawn climbers for decades. The south-facing rock gets plenty of sun, so mornings or late afternoons are comfortable on hot days. Reaching the base means a steep, sustained uphill hike, so travel light and start early.

co_wildcat_one_south_face.blurb: The south face of Wildcat One is the best-developed wall in the Wildcat group of granite outcrops in Unaweep Canyon, south of Grand Junction. Nearly all of its lines are trad, with two bolted routes, and each finishes at a two-bolt anchor above a decent landing. The grades are friendly: a couple of 5.2 to 5.3 beginner routes, a big cluster of 5.7 to 5.9, and a few climbs in the 5.10s and low 5.11s. The routes get shorter from left to right, and some can be top-roped with a 60 meter rope. Newer leaders and families of mixed ability will find a lot to do here.

co_ledges_the.blurb: The Ledges is a tiered roadside cliff in Big Thompson Canyon, in the Estes Park valley, reached by a short scramble from the highway. Almost everything is bolted, with one gear line, and routes mostly fall between 45 and 130 feet. Grades are moderate, from 5.7 to 5.11, and about half the routes cluster in the 5.10 range, with a good number of 5.8 to 5.9s. Climbing here has an adventurous feel: the rock is solid overall but can be loose at the hand level, and each ledge holds loose scree and talus, so belayers need to watch footing and rockfall. Sun reaches the cliff around midday in the busy season.

co_upper_tan_corridor.blurb: The Upper Tan Corridor is the higher half of a granite corridor in Staunton State Park, in the South Platte foothills west of Denver. It was among the first walls developed in the park and holds some of its best moderate-to-hard face climbing. Most of the 27 routes are bolted, with a few trad lines and one top-rope; the grades are concentrated at 5.10 and 5.11, with a handful of 5.12s and 5.13s and one easier route. The climbing is steep and vertical with interesting face holds, and the neighboring corridor routes run roughly 60 to 80 feet. It is a good pick for a 5.10 to 5.11 climber who wants a sport day.

co_right_side_2.blurb: Right Side is the far end of the Golf Wall, a steep limestone sport cliff beside the highway north of Durango. All 27 routes are bolted, and the grades skew hard: a few 5.10s, around a dozen 5.11s and a dozen 5.12s, with nothing really easy. The routes at the Golf Wall are short, roughly 40 to 50 feet, but the steepness makes them pumpy, and the rock quality varies. It is a good option for climbers who want to work at the 5.11 and 5.12 level, and a short hike from the road gets you to the base.
